newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Ssangyong in talks with GM over link-up.
newsitem.headline: Ssangyong in talks with GM over link-up.

text.p: Struggling South Korean auto maker Ssangyong Motor Co Ltd, seeking foreign capital and technology, is in talks with U.S. giant General Motors Corp, company officials said on Thursday.
"General Motors has shown an interest during talks in our sales network for their Korean sales," said a company official, who declined to be identified.
In return, he said Ssangyong was hoping General Motors would inject cash and technology, particularly for developing compact passenger cars.
He emphatically denied media reports that an agreement had been reached. "Everything is in the initial stages. Details are sketchy," he said.

"We are seeking technology from foreign companies, including GM, to make small-sized cars," said a second official, who also declined to be identified. "If we can't get technology, any deal with a foreign company will be pointless."
Mercedes-Benz, a subsidiary of Daimler-Benz AG, has a 2.6 percent-stake in Ssangyong Motor, while parent Ssangyong Group had a 40.2 percent stake in Ssangyong Motor at the end of 1996.
Shares of Ssangyong Motor went limit-up on Thursday, adding 450 won (50 U.S. cents) to 6,170 won ($6.93) on speculation that the Samsung Group wanted to take over the company, brokers said.
The speculation was denied by both groups.
Ssangyong group vice president Cho Nam-do said the automaker expected to slash its losses this year to 150 billion won ($168 million) from 228.5 billion won in 1996.

He said sales were targetted at 2.0 trillion won against 1.37 trillion won last year, largely on the expected strength of demand for its new Korando four-wheel drive utility vehicle and luxury Chairman sedans.
"If the sales target is attained -- and I think it will -- the loss will shrink to 150 billion won this year," Cho said.
Cho said Ssangyong was not considering selling off the vehicle unit because of its problems.
Analysts said they doubted Ssangyong could obtain foreign assistance.
"Why should companies like GM pour money and technology into a loss-making company?" said Kim Byung-joon, an analyst at Dongwon Economic Research Institute.
Ssangyong Motor poured about two trillion won into developing four models, including the Korando and Chairman, in a technical tie-up with Mercedes-Benz.
But just as the company hoped to reap the rewards, South Korea's economy faltered. Domestic car sales slumped last year. Ssangyong Motor puts its total debt at 3.2 trillion won.
Kim at Hyundai estimated the debt figure at 3.7 trillion won, with annual interest payments of 300 billion won.
Sales of utility vehicles are likely to be hit when the government lifts tax breaks on purchases of the popular cars next year. In addition, diesel prices are rising sharply.
"Foreign companies may be only interested in selling their own cars in South Korea through Ssangyong's sales network," said Hur kang, an analyst at Hyundai Securities.
After years of losses, Ssangyong Motor's total shareholders' equity dropped to 33.5 bilion won at the end of 1996, analysts said. They estimated its paid-in capital at 230 billion won.
